## Learning outcomes (SSoQE 2026)

::: callout-tip
### By the end of the week, participants will be able to

- Formulate ecological questions in terms of **exploration**, **inference**, and **prediction**, and choose analysis strategies accordingly.
- Set up and run a **reproducible analysis workflow** (clear project structure, documented steps, and dependency-aware environments).
- Use **version control with Git/GitHub** to track changes, collaborate, and resolve common issues (e.g. merge conflicts).
- Work confidently with ecological data in **R** (import, clean, transform, visualize, and report results).
- Build and interpret common quantitative-ecology analyses across key domains:
  - **Species distributions** (correlative SDMs)
  - **Community ecology** (ordination, dissimilarity, clustering)
  - **Biodiversity patterns** (hypothesis-driven model comparison)
  - **Phylogenetics & macroecology** (trait evolution and diversity patterns)
  - **(Paleo)ecology** (fossil pollen workflows)
  - **Modern modelling** (introductory deep learning workflow)
- Critically evaluate model assumptions, uncertainty, bias, and the limits of prediction.
:::

## What these outcomes map to in the programme

The week is organised into short lectures and hands-on sessions (see the current [Program📅](program.qmd)).
Below is a “skills map” that connects the 2026 sessions to concrete competencies.

### Core workflow skills

- **R workflow basics**: Navigate an IDE, understand environments/sessions, and use R Projects for robust paths.
- **Reproducibility & open science**: Structure projects, keep analyses self-contained, and communicate computational steps clearly.
- **Version control**: Create repositories, commit changes, push/pull, and handle merge conflicts.
- **Collaboration & project management**: Use branches/pull requests, discussions, issues, and task boards to coordinate work.

### Quantitative ecology & modelling

- **Species distribution modelling (I & II)**
  - Obtain occurrence and environmental predictor data and perform basic data-quality checks.
  - Fit a simple correlative SDM (e.g. GLM), evaluate it at a basic level, and project predictions across space and scenarios.

- **Biodiversity and richness**
  - Describe and visualize broad-scale richness patterns.
  - Compare competing hypotheses using model comparison tools (e.g. AIC / Akaike weights) and interpret results.

- **Analysing Community Data (I & II)**
  - Compute community dissimilarity and use ordination methods (e.g. CA / NMDS) to summarize multivariate patterns.
  - Interpret ordination outputs and link community change to time or gradients.

- **Hypothesis testing and null models**
  - Understand why null models are used, what they test, and how results depend on assumptions.
  - Interpret outputs as evidence about processes rather than as “one-number verdicts”.

- **Sample standardisation, resampling, and bias**
  - Recognize common sources of sampling bias and measurement processes in ecological and paleoecological datasets.
  - Understand why standardisation approaches exist and what trade-offs they imply.

### (Paleo)ecology: fossil pollen

- Retrieve fossil pollen records from open databases and handle them in R.
- Visualize pollen data (e.g. pollen diagrams) and build an **age–depth model**.
- Connect paleoecological signals to broader ecological questions.

### Phylogenetics, macroecology, and evolution

- Fit and compare alternative models of trait evolution (e.g. BM vs OU vs EB) and interpret results.
- Use phylogenetic thinking to address non-independence among species.
- Explore how evolutionary history can help explain biodiversity patterns and macroecological structure.

### Deep learning (introductory)

- Explain the basic training/validation workflow for a deep learning model.
- Modify key hyperparameters and interpret changes in model performance.
- Reflect on when deep learning is (and is not) a sensible tool for ecological research.

## Expected background

::: callout-warning
- Basic proficiency in **R** is expected.
- The course is taught in **English**.
:::
